transcript: The family drama is a long standing staple of the American theatrical canon, but The Other Americans at The Public is one of the few I've seen that centers on a Latin American family. The Castros are Colombian American laundromat owners, living in Forest Hills and reeling from a traumatic series of events which they have varying degrees of interest in addressing. A lot of the plot points fall into familiar territory, the kinds of tension-builders and conflict-creators you might expect to see in a family drama, but nothing about this felt stale to me. I partially attribute this to how well the piece interrogates the concept of the American dream, specifically through a Latin American lens, and how it may or may not serve this particular family. The characters are fleshed out, the dialogue flows effortlessly, and the acting is really great — it's always a treat to see such tight ensemble work in a space as intimate as the Anspacher. While parts of it may feel predictable or archetypal, I'd argue that this helps it strike a balance between being a familiar American story and being a distinctly Latin American one. It's hard to make a fresh and original drama, but it's also hard to fault solid writing, acting, and direction. And ultimately, that's what won me over. With that, another Playbill for my collection.
